en: I am neither immortal nor mortal, neither a Daitya nor a Gandharva or Yakṣa, nor a species of Piśāca;
I am neither male, nor female, nor neuter—I am Śiva, whose essential nature is supreme light. (1)

I am neither a child, nor a youth, nor an old man; I am neither an ascetic, nor a student, nor a householder, nor even a forest-dweller, nor one who has renounced worldly duties. I am Śiva, the sole cause of the birth and destruction of the universe. || 2 ||
I am not an object of measurement, for my illusory power (māyā) has been withdrawn; likewise, there is no means to perceive me as something separate.
Though the three bodies are closely embraced [within me], I am Śiva—the non-dual, eternally beyond the senses, and the form of all things. || 3 ||
I am neither the thinker, nor the goer, nor the speaker, nor the doer, nor the enjoyer, nor one established in the stages of life (āśrama);
as I am the very nature of the various modifications of the mind, so too am I Śiva, the illuminator of all mental states. || 4 ||
I have no engagement in the flow of worldly affairs, nor do I have the cessation of evil efforts through the notion of bondage;
since the activity of this mind proceeds from cessation, I am that very essence—the auspicious Śiva.
That which is the cause of the effect of ignorance, whose existence does not manifest by itself without an effect,
and which consists of the light of the beginning, the end, the middle, and the intervals between them— that alone am I.
Since I am not the intellect, there is no failure of my purpose for me; since I am not the body, there is no destruction of my subtle form.
Dwelling in the space of the heart, free from the pain of the three states, I am eternally Śiva, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
That from which the world, through its playfulness, undergoes transformation—that which is the substratum of all modifications—cannot exist as such because of its non-duality;
that from which the activity of the functions of mind, intellect, consciousness, and ego arises, that alone am I.
That which pervades both within and without, eternally pure, that which is the one, ever-present root of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
from which the appearance of the gross and subtle universe arises, and from which its very birth proceeds—that alone am I. 9.
I am that very [Reality] which is the locus of the playful manifestation of the garlands of light-nets of the sun, moon, and lightning; which is devoid of internal differentiation and the like;
in whose nature the entire universe exists as its feet; and from whom the appearance of power arises. 10.

That from which death and time are utterly afraid, from which the play of the mind, intellect, and senses arises, and from which the manifestation of the names of Hari, Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Candra, and others occurs—that alone am I. 11.
That which is all-pervading like space, of peaceful form, the supreme light, devoid of shape, and most excellent;
that which is devoid of beginning and end, the supreme known as Śaṅkara, and that which is to be realized within—that alone am I. 12.
Thus [ends] the work composed by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
The Nirvāṇamañjarī is complete.
